transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-29
Start: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: ~52 min
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE); Maya Chen (Redwood SE); Liam O'Connor (Redwood CSM); Daniel Brooks (Lyric Platform); Sana Iqbal (Lyric SRE); Elena Ruiz (Lyric Head of AI); Marcus Lee (Lyric Security)

Auto Summary (auto-gen, may be rough): quick console demo focusing on request stitching across services, show KV cache misses and fallthroughs, reproduce error paths from logs. Discussed SOC2, KMS, retention. Action items agreed.

[00:00] Jordan Patel: Hey team, thanks for carving out time — uh, quick intro, I'm Jordan, I'm the AE on the account, with Maya — SE, and Liam from success. We'll do a live walk through of Request Chronicle in the Console, show how we stitch traces to logs and do what we call error archaeology.

[00:18] Maya Chen: Hi all, hi Lyric folks. I'll jump into the console share in a sec. Purpose is to show a couple real-world failure cases — one is a KV cache fallthrough that causes a higher-cost model path, and another is an intermittent tokenization error we've seen in similar customers. We'll point out how to surface those in the traces and tie them back to request payloads.

[00:40] Daniel Brooks: Great — for context, our stack is mostly a microservice architecture on EKS, fronted by a gateway that calls Redwood for inference. We keep request payloads for 7 days in our S3 logs and have a centralized ELK stack. Latency SLO is 200ms p95 for internal flows, and cost is very tight.

[01:05] Sana Iqbal: Also to add, we need auditability for certain PII redaction flows; Marcus will flag the compliance concerns later.

[01:15] Marcus Lee: Yep, SOC2 scope and key rotation/KMS usage are big. We prefer Customer-managed keys if possible.

[01:28] Maya Chen: Noted. Ok switching to the Console — can everyone see the Request Chronicle page? I'll start with a high-level request timeline.

[01:45] (screen share begins)

[02:10] Maya Chen: Here is a trace that shows a request spanning the gateway, enrichment job, and then the Redwood inference call. You'll see the request id at the top — we can click and 'stitch logs' to pull in ELK entries by correlating request_id, timestamp and host.

[02:38] Elena Ruiz: Quick question — how reliable is the stitching when clocks skew on our side? We do have some clock drift occasionally.

[02:50] Maya Chen: Good question. The stitching uses a combination of request ID heuristics and a time window; we allow a configurable +/- delta and can fall back to string matching on payload hashes. If your clock skew is more than a few seconds we recommend using a consistent request-id header propagated across services.

[03:20] Jordan Patel: We can also add a small agent rule that normalizes timestamps at ingestion if you want us to demo that in the pilot.

[03:40] (clicks)

[04:00] Maya Chen: Alright, here's the error archaeology view. This is intentionally a bit noisy — the transcript will be rough. You'll see the root path map, and I'm going to drop in two hypothesis markers where the KV cache shows a miss that causes fallback to a larger model.

[04:25] Sana Iqbal: When you say larger model — is that a different model in the same family or a cross-model fallback? We track token count very tightly.

[04:36] Maya Chen: In this case it's a policy we set — if KV cache miss and prompts exceed cached prefix, we route to a safety-model which has higher token usage. You can configure routing to either degrade to a cheaper variant or return a cached partial response.

[05:05] Daniel Brooks: Do you show per-token cost on that timeline? If we accidentally route 40% of traffic to the safety model, that kills our cost targets.

[05:15] Liam O'Connor: Yep, the Console has per-request cost estimators tied to the model and the token delta — you can see an exploded view showing where the extra cost comes in. We'll show an example.

[05:40] Maya Chen: Ok loading a problematic request — note the purple marker is where the KV cache miss occurred. Click 'replay' to see the full request flow.

[06:02] (replay runs, audio playback of request timeline)

[06:25] Maya Chen: Here the request payload had a trailing whitespace character in one of the keys — that caused the cache key to miss. Transcription sometimes shows it as 'white space' or 'white space character' — but you can see the raw payload attached.

[06:45] Daniel Brooks: Oof, small bug on our side — we have some services that canonicalize keys sometimes and sometimes they don't.

[07:00] Maya Chen: Exactly — with Request Chronicle you can pin the raw payload and even diff two requests inline to see the byte-level difference. That makes the 'archaeology' part much faster.

[07:18] Elena Ruiz: Does that raw payload ever contain PII that Redwood stores? We have strict retention policies.

[07:28] Jordan Patel: By default the hosted API will retain logs for X days — we can go over retention and masking. For Private deployments you can configure zero retention in the control plane and have customer-side log storage only. Marcus, that's something for you and our security docs.

[07:52] Marcus Lee: Ok please share the exact retention options and how KMS integrates. We need to see key rotation details.

[08:12] Maya Chen: Will do — I'll attach the Security & Private deployment FAQ.

[08:25] (jump to an example of a non-deterministic error)

[08:40] Maya Chen: This one is interesting — an intermittent tokenization error that only occurs about 0.3% of requests. We aggregate error fingerprints and show frequency across time; you can open the sample set to inspect raw stack traces and correlated logs.

[09:05] Sana Iqbal: Does Redwood capture model-side stack traces? We don't want PII or proprietary prompt text stored.

[09:16] Maya Chen: On hosted, we capture an anonymized model error trace and the minimal required context to reproduce; you can turn off storing prompt text and only keep structured metadata. For Private, you control everything and logs can be ingested only to your S3.

[09:40] (brief crosstalk)

[10:00] Daniel Brooks: Related to latency — how does the Console surface request hot paths? Can we see time spent in network vs time spent in KV cache vs time spent in model inference?

[10:15] Maya Chen: Yes, the flamegraph splits by spans: network, preprocess, KV cache, model, postprocess. You can drill down and export a CSV for p95/p99 analysis. It will break down tokenization time as well.

[10:35] Jordan Patel: A quick note on fallbacks — we support policy-based fallback: region, capacity tier, or model variant. So if a regional pool is saturated, you can force fallback to a cheaper region or a cheaper quantized model. That is important for predictable unit cost.

[11:05] Elena Ruiz: Can you show an example of a canary rollback if a new model causes increased errors? We want automated rollbacks.

[11:18] Maya Chen: Absolutely — here's an A/B rollout in the Console. You can define thresholds (error rate, latency) and automatic rollback rules. If the new model breaches, traffic re-routes to the previous model and a postmortem snapshot is saved with all traces.

[11:45] (shows UI, points at rule config)

[12:10] Daniel Brooks: For the pilot, we want to validate two things: 1) we can reproduce our KV cache miss and fix it, and 2) the p95 latency when using your private deployment in our VPC is under 200ms. How do you suggest we structure the pilot?

[12:28] Jordan Patel: Good asks — pilot plan suggestion: 2-week lab. Week 1: ingestion and request replay with sample traffic to reproduce cache misses. Week 2: deploy Private control plane into your VPC (or use dedicated) and run load tests for latency. We'll include a small runbook for toggling fallback policies.

[12:50] Sana Iqbal: For the private control plane, do we need outbound connectivity? Our environment is air-gapped for some projects.

[13:02] Maya Chen: Private control plane needs no internet egress for inference nodes; the customer-managed control plane can be air-gapped. We do have an optional edge agent for updates, but we can discuss an offline update process.

[13:25] Marcus Lee: Good. We also need audit logs with SAML SSO events tied to user actions.

[13:36] Liam O'Connor: Audit logs and RBAC are part of the enterprise package; we'll include exact retention and export formats in the security packet.

[13:50] (fast-forward to KV cache metrics)

[14:10] Maya Chen: Here are cache hit/miss dashboards. Notice the spike at 03:21 UTC — that correlates with a deploy upstream that changed the canonicalization. You can set alerts on hit ratio and have an automated regression alert in Optimize.

[14:38] Daniel Brooks: Can Optimize suggest quantization or batching changes to reduce cost without touching our model code?

[14:48] Maya Chen: Yes, Optimize analyzes traffic patterns and recommends quant profiles and batching thresholds; it even simulates cost savings given p95 latency targets.

[15:05] Elena Ruiz: One technical nit — when stitching logs, is there any PII redaction step we can add automatically?

[15:15] Maya Chen: We have sanitizers that run during ingestion — regex, structured field masks, and a redaction pipeline. You can configure them and preview sanitized payloads before storage.

[15:35] (customer asks about demo artifacts)

[15:45] Jordan Patel: We'll send the trimmed recording, the security FAQ, and the pilot scope doc. We'll also include a spreadsheet for model routing cost estimations.

[16:05] (short silence, background chatter)

[16:18] Daniel Brooks: A couple of follow-ups — will the Console show when a request was routed across region boundaries? We do multi-region reads and want to see that.

[16:30] Maya Chen: Yep, region tags are embedded in the span metadata; the timeline shows region hops and if a failover happened.

[16:45] Sana Iqbal: Do you support correlation IDs we already generate (not the Redwood request ID)?

[16:55] Maya Chen: Absolutely — you can map your correlation id header to the Redwood request id so everything stitches. We can add that mapping during ingestion.

[17:10] (customer drills into a particular error fingerprint)

[17:25] Maya Chen: This fingerprint shows N different request variants. I'll open the raw payload viewer — see how one of them has an extra control char, that's the common root cause. The Console highlights similar byte sequences across requests.

[17:50] Elena Ruiz: Nice — that would have saved us so much time.

[18:05] Jordan Patel: Quick question — do you have production windows where the inference traffic spikes because of batch jobs? If yes, we can show autoscale policies.

[18:18] Daniel Brooks: Yes, nightly enrichment spikes at 02:00 UTC, and that sometimes collides with daytime traffic in another region.

[18:30] Maya Chen: We have schedule-based autoscaling and burst capacity rules. For dedicated pools you can set reserved capacity for the spike window.

[19:00] (Maya toggles an alert)

[19:15] Maya Chen: Here's an example alert workflow: hit-ratio drops under 70% -> fire an alert -> open the request list -> mark as incident -> assign to owner. It auto-saves the trace snapshot for the postmortem.

[19:40] Marcus Lee: For the audit, does that snapshot include the raw payload? We might need a redacted snapshot.

[19:50] Maya Chen: You can choose snapshot type: full, redacted, metadata-only. We'll recommend redacted for audit exports.

[20:10] (discussion about integration)

[20:30] Daniel Brooks: For the replay capability — can it replay against a staging Redwood model or our in-house runtime?

[20:40] Maya Chen: It can replay to any configured endpoint. For pilot we'd usually point to a staging model in your VPC or a dedicated Redwood staging pool.

[21:00] Elena Ruiz: If we replay queries, will the stimulator include realistic timing to surface race conditions?

[21:12] Maya Chen: You can control inter-request timing distribution; it supports Poisson arrival and fixed bursts so you can approximate production rhythms.

[21:30] (customer asks about billing for pilot)

[21:40] Jordan Patel: Pilot billing is usage-based for hosted; for Private/Dedicated we can do a time-boxed trial with eval credits—I'll include pricing options in the follow-up.

[22:00] Sana Iqbal: Any known limitations with large payloads? We sometimes pass long context windows.

[22:10] Maya Chen: Long context windows increase memory and tokenization time — the Console will show the token breakdown. For really long contexts we recommend prefix caching and segmenting.

[22:30] (customer asks about SSO and audit again)

[22:40] Liam O'Connor: We'll include the SAML SSO integration guide and example audit logs export.

[23:00] (fast-forward, demo wrap-up)

[23:15] Jordan Patel: Ok to wrap — quick recap: Maya will send demo clip + security FAQ; Lyric to send sample request ids; Jordan to send pilot scoping and pricing; schedule pilot kick-off next week. Anyone object?

[23:35] Elena Ruiz: No objections. Sounds good.

[23:42] Daniel Brooks: We'll compile and send the sample payloads by the end of next week.

[23:50] Marcus Lee: I'll add compliance questions to the shared doc.

[24:00] (meeting ends)

Notes about transcript quality: several bits of UI text and product names may be slightly mis-transcribed (e.g., "Request Chronical", "Request Chronicle" may appear inconsistently). There were small periods of cross-talk and background noise during the replay audio.

References shared during call: demo recording link (will be provided), security FAQ doc (links to be sent), pilot scope spreadsheet (to be attached).

End of transcript.
